strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in shadow analysis: existing benchmarks and methods almost exclusively focus on cast shadows, while attached shadows (which carry rich 3D shape and orientation cues) are neglected or lumped together with cast shadows.

The physics-grounded formulation linking light direction and surface normals ($n \cdot \ell > 0$) to generate a partial attached shadow map, integrated into an iterative feedback loop between the shadow detector and light estimator, is conceptually elegant and sound.
Introduces the first curated benchmark specifically annotating cast and attached shadows separately across 1,458 images, incorporating an 'undefined' shadow label to prevent ambiguous supervision.

Quantitative and qualitative results show significant improvements in attached shadow detection (reducing attached shadow BER from ~20-26% down to 12.93%) while maintaining competitive performance on cast and full shadow metrics.
Comprehensive ablation studies validate the benefits of surface normal guidance, multi-step iterative refinement, and individual loss functions.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison fairness: The retrained baseline models (BDRAR, FSDNet, FDRNet, SILT) were trained with full-shadow supervision and separated post-hoc using object masks, whereas the proposed model was trained with multi-class ({bg, cast, attached}) supervision and normal maps. Retraining standard segmentation backbones or baseline detectors directly with 3-class labels (and optionally normal map inputs) would provide a cleaner ablation to isolate the benefit of the physics-grounded iterative loop from simple multi-class training.

Lack of quantitative evaluation on light estimation: While a light estimation module is learned and supervised via geometric heuristics and $L_1$ loss, the manuscript does not evaluate the accuracy of the estimated light direction $\hat{\ell}$ (e.g., mean angular error on the calibrated WSRD subset).

Heuristic light direction pseudo-ground truth: For SOBA and CUHK, light directions are derived heuristically from 2D centroid displacements and relative depth differences. In complex geometries or non-planar receiving surfaces, this heuristic can be noisy and introduce bias into supervision.

Assumption of a single directional light source: Real-world scenes often involve multiple light sources, area lights with soft transitions, or strong ambient illumination, where the binary condition $n \cdot \ell > 0$ does not strictly hold.

strengths: Addresses an important and overlooked problem in shadow analysis: distinguishing attached shadows from cast shadows. While existing shadow detection datasets and methods treat shadows uniformly or focus predominantly on cast shadows, this work highlights the physical and geometric distinction of attached shadows.

The proposed closed-loop framework is physically sound and well-motivated. Exploiting the interaction between surface normals and light direction ($n \cdot \ell > 0$) to generate a partial attached shadow prior that iteratively refines segmentation and lighting estimation is intuitive and effective.
Introduction of a dedicated, manually annotated benchmark of 1,458 images with explicit separation of cast and attached shadows, providing a valuable resource for future research in this direction.

Comprehensive empirical validation: the proposed approach significantly outperforms prior methods retrained on the benchmark, reducing attached shadow BER by more than 33% (from ~19.5-26.6% down to 12.93%) while maintaining competitive cast shadow performance.
Thorough ablation studies analyzing the impact of geometric guidance, number of iterations, and distinct loss components, accompanied by a candid discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: The 3D light direction supervision relies heavily on heuristics for the majority of the dataset (SOBA and CUHK subsets), computed from 2D object-shadow centroid displacements and relative depth. This approximation can introduce noisy supervision into $\mathcal{L}_{dir}$.

The paper does not report quantitative evaluation of the estimated 3D light directions (e.g., mean angular error), particularly on calibrated subsets such as WSRD, making it difficult to assess how accurately the light estimator actually performs in isolation.
The single directional light assumption restricts the applicability of the formulation in complex scenes with multiple light sources or strong diffuse ambient lighting.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in shadow analysis: distinguishing between cast and attached shadows, whereas existing deep learning literature predominantly focuses on cast shadows.

The physically grounded formulation integrating surface normals, directional lighting ($n \cdot \ell > 0$), and shadow segmentation into an iterative closed-loop refinement framework is conceptually sound and well-motivated.
Introduces a dedicated benchmark of 1,458 images with cast/attached shadow masks and an 'undefined' shadow label to properly handle ambiguous background shadows during training and evaluation.
Comprehensive ablation study (Table 3) that clearly breaks down the individual contributions of normal guidance, iterative refinement steps, and specific loss components.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline protocol: Existing baselines were only retrained using binary full-shadow supervision and separated post-hoc using object masks. Standard multi-class segmentation baselines (e.g., SegFormer, Mask2Former, or SILT modified directly for 3-class segmentation with and without normal maps) are not included to isolate the contribution of the physical prior from modern general segmentation architectures.

Heuristic light direction supervision: For SOBA and CUHK subsets, the ground-truth light direction $\ell^*$ is derived via a heuristic based on 2D object-to-shadow centroid displacement and monocular relative depth. Training with an $\ell_1$ loss against this heuristic target may inject considerable bias into the light estimator.

Lack of quantitative evaluation on light estimation: Despite proposing joint shadow detection and light estimation, the paper does not report any metric (such as mean angular error) evaluating the accuracy of the predicted 3D light vectors, even on datasets with known ground truth such as WSRD.

Technical details on iterative training are underspecified: It is unclear whether gradients are backpropagated across unrolled iterations (recurrent training) or if stop-gradient is applied between iterations.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in shadow analysis: distinguishing between cast and attached shadows, which have distinctly different physical formation mechanisms and visual characteristics.

The physical formulation is principled and intuitive: using estimated 3D directional illumination and surface normals to compute an initial attached shadow prior (surfaces facing away from the light source) and coupling this with shadow detection in a closed iterative feedback loop.

Valuable dataset contribution: curating and manually refining a dataset of 1,458 images with separate annotations for cast and attached shadows, accompanied by surface normals and light directions, which fills a clear benchmark gap.

Thorough empirical evaluation: compares against seven state-of-the-art shadow detectors (both pretrained and retrained), provides extensive ablations (geometry input, number of feedback iterations, loss functions), includes cross-dataset generalization experiments on images/videos, and validates utility on downstream shadow removal via a user study.
weaknesses: Simplified illumination assumption: assuming a single distant directional light source limits applicability to complex environments with multiple light sources, diffused/ambient illumination, or complex indoor geometries where cast shadows from secondary occluders dominate.

Heuristic ground truth for light direction: for SOBA and CUHK subsets, light vectors are derived via 2D centroid-to-shadow displacement and relative depth signs, which can be noisy or imprecise for non-convex objects or uneven ground planes.

Sensitivity to upstream depth and surface normal quality: because the partial attached shadow map directly depends on normal orientations, errors or inversions from monocular depth estimators (e.g., Depth-Anything-V2) can propagate directly into false attached shadow predictions.

Trade-off on cast shadow BER: while attached shadow BER improves significantly over retrained baselines, cast shadow BER is slightly higher than the retrained SILT baseline (5.04 vs. 4.52), although cast F1 is notably improved (85.46 vs. 68.31). A deeper discussion of this trade-off would strengthen the analysis.

strengths: Addresses an important and historically overlooked problem in shadow detection: explicitly disentangling attached shadows from cast shadows, which has direct downstream benefits (e.g., in shadow removal and 3D perception).

Grounded physical modeling: the mutual coupling between 3D directional light estimation and surface normals to compute partial attached shadow priors through an iterative feedback loop is elegant, intuitive, and technically sound.

Significant empirical performance gains: achieves a marked reduction in attached shadow BER (over 33% relative reduction compared to retrained baselines) while retaining competitive full and cast shadow metrics.

Valuable benchmark contribution: curates and manually refines a dataset of 1,458 images with separated cast and attached shadow masks, light directions, and normals, addressing a clear data void in the literature.
Thorough ablation studies and practical downstream validation, including a well-designed user study on shadow removal demonstrating the benefit of separate attached shadow refinement.
weaknesses: Heuristic ground truth for light direction: For the majority of images (from SOBA and CUHK), the pseudo-ground-truth light direction is derived from 2D centroid displacements and monocular relative depth differences, which can introduce systematic bias into the lighting supervision.

Heavy reliance on upstream foundation models: The approach depends strictly on the quality of predicted depths and surface normals (from Depth-Anything-V2). Although acknowledged in the limitations, there is no quantitative sensitivity analysis regarding how depth/normal degradation impacts final segmentation.

Single directional light assumption: The framework assumes a single distant directional light source. While fitting for sunny outdoor and single-source indoor scenarios, it limits applicability to diffuse/overcast conditions or multi-source indoor environments.

strengths: Relevant and under-explored problem: Differentiating attached shadows from cast shadows is physically and perceptually important, yet most existing deep shadow detection methods conflate them into a single binary mask.

Physically grounded formulation: The core concept of establishing a closed feedback loop between light direction estimation, surface normals, and shadow segmentation is conceptually elegant and physically intuitive.

Dataset contribution: The authors curate and annotate a benchmark of 1,458 images with explicit cast and attached shadow labels, paired with normal maps and light directions, which fills an important gap in the shadow literature.

Practical downstream demonstration: The paper effectively illustrates the practical utility of separating shadow types in shadow removal, showing that refining attached shadow regions separately prevents undesirable over-attenuation of object surfaces (supported by a user study).

Detailed ablation studies: The submission includes comprehensive ablations examining the impact of surface normals, number of feedback iterations, individual loss terms, inference runtime, and qualitative cross-dataset transfer on videos.
weaknesses: Unfair/incomplete baseline comparisons: The primary baselines (BDRAR, FSDNet, FDRNet, SILT) are binary shadow detectors whose predictions are post-processed into cast and attached components simply using an object mask. The paper lacks comparison against modern generic multi-class segmentation baselines (e.g., Mask2Former, SegFormer, or DeepLabV3+) trained directly on the proposed 3-class {background, cast, attached} labels with RGB and RGB+Normal inputs.

Heuristic ground truth for light direction supervision: For over 85% of the dataset (SOBA and CUHK subsets), ground truth 3D light vectors are estimated via an ad-hoc heuristic based on object-shadow 2D centroid offsets and depth differences. In scenes with complex object geometry, non-planar ground, or perspective distortion, this heuristic introduces systematic errors, making direct supervision via L_dir questionable.

Overly simplified physical assumptions: The formulation relies on a single scene-wide directional light source and approximates attached shadows purely via n · l > 0. This formulation fails to account for diffuse ambient skylight, multi-light indoor setups, or self-occlusion/geometric blocking on complex surfaces.

Restricted evaluation scope: Because undefined shadows outside the foreground objects are excluded from the cast/attached evaluation, the benchmarks only evaluate foreground object regions rather than full-scene shadow decomposition.

Strong dependence on pre-trained foundation models: The pipeline relies heavily on Depth-Anything-V2 and gradient-based normal derivation, as well as BiRefNet for object masks. When normal predictions are noisy or flipped (as acknowledged in Section 6), detection performance degrades substantially.
